'''Andras (Andrew) Keller''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref name="frs">{{Cite journal | last1 = Windle | first1 = A. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2001.0017  | doi-access = free| title = Andrew Keller. 22 August 1925 - 7 February 1999: Elected F.R.S. 1972 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 47 | pages = 293 | year = 2001 | s2cid = 70950680 }}</ref><ref name=indie>{{Cite news|last=Hoffman|first=John D|title=Obituary: Professor Andrew Keller|newspaper=The Independent|date=29 March 1999}}</ref> (22 August 1925 &ndash; 7 February 1999) was a naturalized [[Great Britain|British]] polymer scientist.  He was  Research Professor in Polymer Science, Department of Physics, [[University of Bristol]], 1969–91, then [[professor emeritus]].

==Biography==

Andras Keller was born in [[Budapest]], the only child of [[Jew]]ish parents. He entered the [[Eötvös Loránd University|University of Budapest]] in 1943, and gained his BSc in chemistry cum laude in 1947. He began his PhD studies at the same university but his work was interrupted by the rapidly deteriorating political situation in Hungary in 1948. He fled to England, leaving behind a submitted but unexamined PhD thesis.<ref name="frs"/><ref name=windle>{{Cite journal|last=Windle|first=A F|title=Obituary: Andrew Keller FRS 1925-1999|journal=Journal of Materials Science|volume=35|page=5017|date=2000|issue=20|doi=10.1023/A:1004867312192|s2cid=135663513|doi-access=free}}</ref>

He took a position with [[Imperial Chemical Industries]] in [[Manchester]], as technical officer in the Polymers Division, where he was given the task of working out how the physical structure of
polymers affects crystallization. In 1955, he moved to the [[University of Bristol]] Physics Department as Research Assistant, under [[Frederick Charles Frank|Charles Frank]], heading a team financed by the [[Ministry of Supply]] (later Ministry of Aviation). Here, he began to further develop his ideas on crystallisation, and obtained his PhD in 1958.<ref name="frs"/> Meanwhile, Keller had become a naturalized citizen of the UK in 1954<ref name="indie"/> or 1955.<ref name=guardian>{{Cite news|last1=Barham|first1=Peter|last2=Odel|first2=Jeff|title=Andrew Keller: A pioneer of polymer physics|newspaper=The Guardian|date=13 May 1999}}</ref>

A key part of his work at Bristol was his discovery in 1957 of [[Crystallization of polymers|chain folding in polymer crystals]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Keller|first=A|title=A note on single crystals in polymers: Evidence for a folded chain configuration|journal=Philosophical Magazine|volume=2|issue=21|pages=1171–1175|date=September 1957|doi=10.1080/14786435708242746|bibcode=1957PMag....2.1171K}}</ref> The findings were not universally accepted however, and there was much debate between opposing camps for many years to come. It came to a head at a [[Faraday Discussions|Faraday Discussion]] in Cambridge in 1979.<ref>{{Cite journal|editor-last=Young|editor-first=D A|title=Crystalline polymers; an introduction|journal= Faraday Discussions of the Chemical Society|volume=68|page=145|location=London|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|date=1979|doi=10.1039/dc9796800145}}</ref> It was an important meeting because “The arguments thereafter moved from whether one believed in regular chain folding, or in no chain folding at all, to issues of the degree of regularity of the folding under the specific conditions of solidification of a particular material.”<ref name="frs"/>

Keller retired in 1991. The occasion was marked by a conference that year on polymer physics at Bristol.<ref>{{Cite web|title= Catalogue description: Conference on Polymer Physics to mark the Retirement of Andrew Keller FRS, Bristol, 3-5 April 1991|website=The National Archives|url= https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/2fe38b1e-8f8d-4921-b971-dff2e2e7e0e7|access-date=31 October 2020}}</ref>

===Family===

Keller met Eva Bulhack, a [[Transylvanian Saxons|Transylvanian Saxon]] from Romania, in England. They married in 1951, and had two children: Peter and Nicola.

Andrew Keller died of a heart attack on 7 February 1999 while on a skiing holiday in Switzerland.<ref name=guardian/>

==Honours and awards==

*1964  High Polymer Physics Prize, [[American Physical Society]]
*1969  Prize of Materials Science Club of Great Britain
*1972  Fellow of The [[Royal Society]]
*1975  Swinburne Medal of the [[Institute of Materials, Minerals and Mining|Plastics and Rubber Institute]], London
*1980  Centennial Scholar and Medal, [[Case Western Reserve University|Case Institute of Technology]], Cleveland, Ohio
*1981  Clyde Medal of the [[University of Utah]]
*1983  [[Max Born Medal and Prize]]
*1983  Fraser Price Memorial Award, [[University of Massachusetts Amherst|University of Massachusetts]]
*1984  [[Rumford Medal]] of The Royal Society
*1984  Medal of the [[Collège de France]], Paris
*1994  Elected member of the [[Academia Europaea]]
*1998  Elected External Member of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]]
}}
